speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT JAMES MANION (Fort William and Rainy River) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is advisable that the Government should bring forward a policy having for its object the development of the natural resources of Canada.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, only the importance of the subject of the development of the natural resources of this country would make me presume upon the patience of the House even for a short time to take up this question again; but I am so impressed with its importance, and so impressed with the fact that it is the duty of the Government and of this House to work out some policy whereby we may bring about greater development of our natural resources, that I am taking the liberty of once again dealing with this subject.
If one may judge by the many speeches made throughout this country by members of the different political parties in which this question is refered to and by the kindly reception with which the remarks on this question are always received, one must come to the conclusion that it is at least a popular subject. It is worth while, however, to remember that a pound of action is worth a ton of oration, and unless some of these orations are implemented by action, it would be as well that the speeches had never been made. I feel sure that the party which works out some scheme whereby these natural resources will be developed will meet with the applause and approval of the people of this country. I admit it is not an easy question to work out but I believe that if the best of brains of this House are applied to it, it can be done.
Just to illustrate the possibilities in some parts of Canada where the land is looked upon as more or less barren, I am going to quote a statement made to me by Mr. Stefansson, in which he shows the meat producing possibilities of Canada's northern lands to be among the greatest in the
world. His statement boiled down is as follows:
North Alaska and Northern Canada have the same climate, vegetation and general natural conditions. Therefore, they have they same possibilities.
Between 1892 and 1902, 1280 reindeer were imported into Alaska. Since 1892 they have butchered more than 100,000. They now have 200,000 living animals and by the middle of May they will have from 260,000 to 275,000.
The Department of Education at Washington was handling the experiment, as the reindeer were introduced to benefit the Eskimos. Last year the Government at Washington began to realize its importance as an industry, rather than philanthropy. They appropriated {25,000 to study the conditions. They came to Ottawa and took our greatest authority on parasitic diseases Dr. Hadwin, of the Department of Agriculture here; got an American Grazing Expert and with Dr. E. W. Nelson, Chief of the United States Biological Survey reported on the industry. They visited Alaska. Dr. Nelson has returned and has testified before the Agricultural Appropriation Committee of Congress that the increase of reindeer in the future will undoubtedly be more rapid than in the past, (due to bad handling) until all available land in Alaska is covered. He says there will be 5,000,000 reindeer in Alaska in 1935. This will allow for the butchering after 1935 of 1,250,000 per year, equivalent to about 3,000,000 carcases of sheep.
The export of reindeer meat began four years ago to Seatle; the sale the first year was a failure, but the last three years it has been very successful. In 1919 dressed carcasses sold at Nome, Alaska, for 22c per lb. In 1920 though beef was going down, reindeer has gone up to 24c per lb., f.o.b., steamer at Nome. In 1920 there were 1,600 carcases sold or 150 tons. Small sales are due to large local consumption and limited freezer capacity of steamers. They figure on shipping 500 tons in 1921.
Mr. Stefansson concludes that Northern Canada, having 2,000,000 square miles as against Alaska's 200,000 has tremendous possibilities for meat producing.
It might be well to point out that in 1919 there were forty-eight million sheep in the whole of the United States. The extract I have read has no particular reference to the question with which I am dealing, but I quote it because it shows the possibility for development of some of what are considered barren lands of this country.
Now to get back to the question of mineral development which I was discussing. Raw materials are the basic elements of commercial progress, and Canada, possessing raw materials in such vast abundance, has an immense advantage over those countries that are not so fortunately endowed. While some of our natural resources such as agriculture, are being developed to a great extent in this country, I consider that the iron, coal and oil resources are being neglected. If you will study the commercial history of any of the great commercial countries of the world,

States has a population of one hundred and ten million. One reason for the great population in the country to the South is that their natural resources have been developed and their commercial and industrial life built up, partly by our assistance. I believe it is time that we in this country endeavoured to develop our own natural resources, and not leave to posterity this development and the prosperity incident thereto.
An increase of population is one of our greatest needs, and yet our population is not growing as it should. Agnes Laut in Maclean's Magazine of January 15th, 1921 says:
In spite of newspaper reports our Immigation is not increasing. It is decreasing. If you count up the number of Americans who registered at Ports of entry in Canada from the Klondike boom to the War, you will find the total something between one million and a quarter and one million and one-half. If you then figure up how many Americans remained in Canada you will find the total about 440,000.
There is another point which makes this question of the utmost importance, and that is the railway question in Canada. Unfortunately our railway situation forms a very important problem to the people of this country. We have built our railways twenty or thirty years in advance of our time, resulting in duplication and over-development. We have forty thousand miles of railway of which over one-half is in the hands of the Canadian people. It might he worth while to compare the figures of the Canadian railway system with those of other countries. Canada has one mile of railway to every 200 persons; United States has one mile to every 400 persons; Great Britain has one mile to every 2,000 persons; and Russia has one mile to every 4,000 persons. Canada has four or five times the mileage of railway that Japan has, with a population of 56,000,000; three times the mileage of Italy with a population of
36,000,000, a greater mileage than Great Britain with 45,000,000; or than France with 40,000,000; and equal to that of Germany with 65,000,000. These figures illustrate the over-development of our railways. We have not the population to provide traffic, that is passenger and freight traffic, for our railways. Mineral development would help us to secure railway traffic. In the United States forty-seven per cent of the freight traffic on the railways comes from the mines. In Canada the percentage is very much less. I have discussed this question with some of the higher officials, of the Canadian National Railways and they are of opinion that it is of prime im- I c
portance to the railways of this country. One of them, an important Canadian National Railways official, writing to me a few days ago, used the following words:
I am keenly interested in this subject which I believe is a vital matter to the Canadian National Railways: in fact I do not know anything of greater importance to Canada as a whole than the development of our iron resources.
There is another side to this question and that concerns not only iron but coal and oil. The iron, coal and oil supplies of the world are not inexhaustible and the time may arrive when the United States may see fit to put an embargo on iron ore, as it has in the past proposed imposing an embargo on coal. If they did that the steel plants in this country would have to close down, in my opinion, with the exception of those in Nova Scotia which get their supply from Wabana, Newfoundland. That would place Canada in a very difficult position. The late James J. Hill, writing in 1910 upon the iron deposits in the United States, said they would be depleted within twenty-five to fifty years. Taking these facts into account surely it is worth while for the people of this country to endeavour to place themselves in an independent commercial position so far as the United States is concerned.
The objection is urged that we have a coal shortage in this country and that we have not the necessary fuel to smelt the iron. In answer to that I would say that Canada in the matter of coal deposits is the second richest country in the world, she is second only to the United States. It is true that it is a transportation problem to get that coal from the extreme East and the extreme West to the central parts of Canada; but I believe the day is coming when we will be able to take the coal from Nova Scotia up to the head of the Great Lakes, and bring it from the Prairie Provinces to the same point, and then we shall be able to develop our iron deposits with coal from our own coal mines. Then there is the fact to be considered that in this country there is some 18,000,000 horsepower of potential electricity of which only about 2,000,000 is now being developed. In some countries in the world electricity is being used for smelting purposes. To a certain extent it has been found expensive for that purpose; nevertheless one concern, the Canadian Steel Forgings of Toronto, and a few other firms, are using electricity for smelting purposes in this country.

In closing you may ask me what I propose after these preliminary remarks. Many schemes have been advanced for the solution of this question. I only mention some of them, as follows:	1. A tariff
against the importation of iron ore; 2. A bounty on Canadian ore; 3. Financing private corporations; 4. Co-operation with private corporations; or, 5, a thorough investigation. I repeat, Sir, that no scientific or thorough investigation has ever been made that I know of into the Canadian iron ore question, and that proposition would not meet with opposition. I believe that all the parties in this House would deem it only fair for the Government to look into the question even if they spent considerable money in so doing. We have expended considerable on the lignite question in Western Canada. I commend the Government for that action and I wish them to follow the same course in regard to Canadian iron ores. In my final words I would say:	Let some action
be taken, for this is one of the methods by which we will help to increase our population; make a .market for our agricultural products; give employment to our people; provide freight for our over developed railways; make ourselves commercially independent of the United States; and generally help to put Canada in its proper place among the advancing industrial nations of the world.

It is with a great deal of pleasure
indeed that I second the motion moved by my hon. friend from Fort William. He has descanted interestingly and well on the iron resources of Canada and he is much more competent to speak on the subject than I am. One thing however, that he said, particularly interested me. That was his comparison of the Canadian situation with the American situation, in connection with which he showed that the American corporations engaged in these industries are tremendously more capitalized than our smaller industries in Canada. There is no question, Mr. Speaker, that capital plays a very important part in the development of these undertakings. A properly organized industry with a capitalization of $100,000,000 as many of these American companies are, is much more influential in the markets of the world than a less efficiently organized body with a smaller capital. As a matter of fact there is no comparison at all, and recognizing the tremendous problem that confronts us in the mining and manufacturing of our iron deposits, we must take some action as a government and try to equalize conditions as between our own country and foreign countries. Faced as we are with these enormous imports of iron and steel products from foreign countries, we cannot afford to stand idly by and allow our natural resources to be neglected while other countries prosper at our expense.
In supporting the motion presented by my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion), I wish to put the broadest possible interpretation upon the term " natural resources." I do not restrict it to the mining of iron, lead, zinc, copper or other minerals; I would so broaden our policy that we should develop to the furthest limit the manufacture at home of these and other natural resources. To me the mining of iron or any other metal means blast furnaces, refineries, rolling mills, stamping mills, and everything else necessary to carry that particular metal to its complete manufactured state. That means employment in Canada for vast numbers of expert workmen. As one who in my younger days worked with the workmen of Canada and spent my time as a workman amongst them, I came to know fairly well what they are, and my experience also covered some five years working among workmen in foreign countries, which enabled me to compare our own workmen with foreign workmen. As a result of my experience and observation I say unhesitatingly that in intelligence, application and honesty of service to those who employ them our Canadian workmen have no superiors. To-day our workmen are satisfied with the laws and the institutions of Canada, and it is their desire to remain in the Dominion. The only thing they object to is that they have not the opportunities here that they can get in a big country like the United States, which is so highly developed. Not having those opportunities at home, and desirous of succeeding in life, naturally they go to that country, as my hon. friend from Fort William has said.' Therefore we need a domestic policy which will give our workmen the opportunities here which they now must seek abroad and which will give them a share in the building up of this Dominion.
Our nataural resources are not confined to minerals; they include our agricultural lands, and this is what I am most particularly interested in because in the western country these lands are our chief natural

ceramic engineer, whose whole time would be devoted to the work, would result in an undreamed-of development of one of Saskatchewan's greatest natural resources.
I ask that we co-operate with the provincial governments in the work they are now undertaking. It is not sufficient that we should make investigations and reports, without drawing the attention of the investing public to the necessity for the development of these great natural resources. Pottery, earthenware, tile-these things we import in large quantities into Western Canada. What has been the cause? You all know that these things carry a very high freight classification, and the result is that we have to pay enormous prices for what we buy. That particularly is the case since the various bodies interested in increasing freight rates practised lynch law and strangled Canadian business, as they have done recently, by the increase in rates.
I now wish to come to another of our resources spoken of by my hon. friend- coal. We have enormous quantities of coal in Western Canada-so great that the amount is really beyond computation. Some of these coal mines-well, it is almost dangerous to speak of them, because people will hardly believe what you tell them. I have before me, however, a report issued by our own Government with respect to a mine which is on the bor-
4 p.m. der between Alberta and British Columbia. This mine, which has really not yet been opened up contains the finest of anthracite coal, according to a government analysis. The total amount of coal in this particular mine which has not yet been touched-and which, I believe, is the property of Pat Burns, of Calgary, and his company-the total amount of coal known to be there is 21,570,000,000 tons. Suppose there were only half that amount, or 10,000,000,000 tons. Working 313 days in the year on the basis of an output of 5,000 tons a day, there would be a total output of 1,565,000 tons per year-an amount which would supply practically all the anthracite coal consumed in Canada. At that rate we would have enough in that one mine to last 6,640 years-and this is according to the report of our Federal Government. Well, with such figures before us, what are we going to do?
During the week-end I read an interesting account of a meeting of the Mining Institute held in Montreal. I quote the following from an article written by the
FMr. Cowan.]
editor of the Mining Journal, who is also, I think, president of the Mining Institute:
That western coal is the guarantee of our national independence was the declaration made to-day at the Canadian Club luncheon by F. W. Gray, editor of Canadian Mining Journal who was speaking on "The Commercial and National Assets of the Canadian Coal Supply."
Mr. Gray said that in the west lies the future workshop of Canada and that Canada had 17 per cent of the world's supply and 71 per cent of the Empire's supply of coal. The maritime provinces contained 0.7 per cent of our coal reserves, he said, all good bitimunious coal, while the western fields contained the balance.
What ground has he for making such an assertion? If we go to Great Britain, we find that she has enormous deposits of coal. I suppose the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) would say that Great Britain's industrial supremacy depends upon free trade. In my opinion, it has depended, and to-day depends, entirely upon the fact that she has enormous coal deposits, and around that coal area have been built up the biggest industries of the world. If we look at the situation in America, we find a similar condition of affairs in Pennsylvania, Montana, Ohio; wherever you find coal deposits, you find large steel plants and enormous industries growing up around them. As my hon. friend has pointed out this afternoon, in Sydney, Cape Breton, you will find an enormous industrial development. And why? Simply and solely because great deposits of coal are to be found there. Is it then unreasonable for us to say that in Western Canada, with our coal deposits, exactly the same thing will happen as has happened everywhere else? Therefore, I firmly believe that we should have some department of Government which will take a statement such as this, coming from a man thoroughly qualified to speak on the subject and give it such prominence in the various journals of the world, wherever indeed there is a body of men who have money which they wish to invest in enterprises like this, that their attention may be drawn to the matter and that we may receive some benefit therefrom.
My hon. friend referred to briquettes. Let me express as strongly as I can my appreciation of the action taken by the Government in starting a briquetting plant. I understand it is now nearly completed, and I am satisfied that the $600,000 odd spent on it is going to result in great benefit to Western Canada. Three Governments acted in co-operation with regard to that plant and that seems to be a very

proper procedure to follow. Why should we have anything but co-operation amongst the Governments of this Dominion, especially in such matters as this? But it must be remembered that the manufacture of briquettes there is only a small part of the game, and I sincerely hope that the Lignite Utilization Board continue their work of experimentation until they are able to manufacture the by-products, many of which can be manufactured there into something of value to the Dominion of Canada.
Just recently a new discovery of coal has been made at Lampman, bordering on the Moose mountains. Geologists have told me very bluntly that it is absolutely impossible for a grade of coal such as is being taken out of that mine to exist there; that it cannot be done; that the coal is not there. But the fact is that the coal is there. It is now proved to be there to the extent of millions of tons, how many millions we do not yet know. This is a high grade of coking coal. And what does chat mean? My hon. friend spoke about bringing coal from the West to the head of the lakes. Through this discovery, the highest grade of coking coal has been brought, by one jump, 600 miles nearer the province of Ontario than was dreamed of a little while ago. That is a very susbstantial number of miles to knock off the haulage of coal. Two years ago the Government put a line of railway into the new coal field, and to-day the rails are being laid thereon. I hope it will be completed this summer because I am satisfied that it is going to be of great assistance in the development of the Moose mountain coal deposits.
Just in conclusion, I want to say this. While from Western Canada for many years back has come a very vigorous denunciation of everything in the shape of capitalism, big interests, manufacturers money derived in any way except by working the soil, there has been growing up amongst the young men of Western Canada an entirely different spirit and to-day they are calling for industrial development and new industries. In support of that, I am going to read an extract from an editorial from a western paper supporting what has been done by the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan, both of which in the past year have established industrial departments:
The Alberta Legislative Assembly on Wednesday unanimously endorsed the proposal of the government to aid in the campaign for
the promotion and development of Alberta's industries, some members expressing the view that the sum should be $50,000 instead of $20,000 as provided in the estimates.
That is for industrial development.
It may be taken for certain that as a result of
the propaganda of Alberta, capital will be attracted to the development of her industries, and industrial population drawn to the province and more enterprise and scientific and business methods employed in the exploitation of the resources already at command. It believes the Federal government has a responsibility towards the natural resources of the country as a whole and a relationship to observe in the supply of essential raw materials within the empire. For that reason it favors the establishment of a new ministry with a national objective and carrying with it a national prestige in order that Canada may be in a position to control the home market and to enter effectively into competition in foreign markets.
They ask for a new minister, but I am not going to go as far as that; I believe that would be an unnecessary step at the present time. But our Government should take every possible means to further the development of the natural resources of Canada through some department especially instructed so to do.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac) : Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to congratulate the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) for introducing this resolution condemning the Government for their inactivity and lack of policy in regard to the natural resources of the country. His resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is advisable that the Government should bring forward a policy having for its object the development of the natural resources of Canada.
I think that is deserving of consideration, not so much of the Government as of the people of Canada, who are waiting for an opportunity to take advantage of every means of promoting the development of the country. My hon. friend pointed out that the accomplishment of this Government with regard to the development of the natural resources of Canada consisted so far in giving a lease to a gentleman named Stefansson to raise reindeer in the - far North. You will not be surprised, Mr. Speaker, if you learn very soon that Mr. Stefansson's ranch will not materialise into anything of great consequence to the people of Canada. It is more probable that the Hudson's Bay Company will find themselves in conflict with Mr. Stefansson in his lease and that they will find it necessary to buy him out, and that will be last of the reindeer enterprise in this country.



My hon. friend in his good Tory way suggests that there should be a bounty. These enterprises always get back to the same basis with the Tories; they must find a way getting to the treasury of Canada for their friends. With them there is no other way of developing the country than by leading their friends to the treasury; that is the simple and easy way, and while the people, of course, must suffer, that is not a matter of any consequence to our Tory friends.

The hon. member has
already made so many misstatements of what I have said that, before he goes any further, I had better correct his last one. I did not suggest a bounty; I suggested an investigation.

My hon. friend suggested a bounty in a resolution which he moved last year. I suppose he has changed his mind. That is the privilege of the hon. gentleman. Before he sat down he suggested that a bounty might be a means, but that an investigation should be held. We, of course, are all agreed that an investigation of the Government should be held at any time. It all comes back to the same old plan of getting at the treasury of going to the trough.
My hon. friend was quite right in criticising the Government for the lack of an energetic immigration policy. How can we hope to develop the resources of this country with a policy of emigration, not immigration? We are spending a great deal of money on an immigration policy, and the sum total of our efforts has been that people are leaving this country faster than they are coming in. My hon. friend pointed that out in the statement of Agnes Laut in Maclean's Magazine. We are giving the people every possible assistance in leaving. We are doing everything we can in Western Canada to get rid of probably the best farmers in the country-the Men-nonites. We are doing everything we can to drive them out of the country. I saw in the local press a few days ago the statement at a banquet by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) that three or four ship loads of Poles had been turned back from the shores of Canada. They had landed here and then were told to go back home. That is our immigration policy apparently. Then I notice in this morning's newspaper that some 5,000 or 6,000 of the Six Nations Indians are looking for a home in the United States because they can place no dependence on the laws of Canada. The Canadian Government is driving

everybody out, and the few that are left they would tax out of the country.
My hon. friend speaks of railway difficulties in the way of the development of our natural resources. Why, the only solution of the question is immigration and production. If we have overbuilt our railways, we must get people producing on the land, and in the forests, the mines, and fisheries; but you cannot hope to get them if you build up a tariff wall against everything they would bring into this country, and make living conditions such that they cannot face the future here. You cannot tax yourself rich; you can only tax yourself poor. If you attempt to tax people to promote every kind of enterprise in the country, you get to the stage where the taxpayers are unable to bear the burden. My hon. friend is simply following his leader in promoting the idea of taxing every person for the benefit of the special interests. They have their special friends who must be taken care of, by taxation or otherwise. These special friends must be looked after because they are looking after the Government^ naturally the Government in turn attempts to support its friends -to lead them to the treasury. That has always been the Tory policy in this country, and it is the policy that has brought the country to the condition it is in today, with an enormous debt and an excessive taxation. The expenditure of the Tory party since they came into power in 1911, exclusive of the war, has been greater than the total expenditure of previous Governments for forty years. But still they continue on that basis, hoping to bring people in by telling them that they are going to tax industry and everything that a man wants to use, just to bolster up their friends in some enterprise. My hon. friend knows, or should know, that his own territory of New Ontario is not being developed. Why? Because you won't allow the people who would develop it to go in there. My hon. friend knows there are only certain classes of people who will settle in Northern Ontario and develop its resources.
Who are they?
Principally the French-Canadian, and the Scandinavians. They are the only two classes of people who will go into that class of country and develop it.
Why are they prevented?

Because Mr. Ferguson
passed legislation in Ontario, excluding the

French-Canadians from Ontario. They are told not to settle in that country. I see the leader of the Government would hold out an olive branch-

They are the friends of my right hon. friend more than mine. They are a combination of Tories and U.F.O.- a sort of reformed Tory party in Ontario. It would not be bad business for the Department of Immigration and Colonization of this Government to try and regulate to some extent the foolish legislation that has been passed in some of these provinces. We have spent great sums of money to develop Northern Ontario, and then the Ontario Government comes along and cuts off any possibility of that investment being a success.

By prohibiting the French Canadians from coming in.
Mr. KEiSFER:	What legislation prohibits them.

My hon. friend's leader
in Ontario, Mr. Howard Ferguson, prohibits any Frenchman from occupying land there. He passed a law that allowed the government to take his land away if he could not speak English, if you please, whereas English is no more the language of this country than French is. The French people have the same right to insist on their language as the leading language, as English-speaking people have on theirs. But my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) would not see that as the situation. It would suit his election purposes better to have Mr. Ferguson's legislation on the statute books, just as it would suit my right hon. friend the leader of this Government better. He made use of just such legislation as that at the last election, and he will make use of it again in the coming election. He will make use of it anywhere he can in Canada, just as he and the Tory party have done in the past.

May I ask
a question? Does my hon. friend take the responsibility of saying that Mr. Ferguson passed a law prohibiting French-speaking people settling in Ontario because they did not speak the English language?

When was that legislation passed?

If my hon. friend was
asleep at the time, I Was not. It was passed in 1915. If my hon. friend wants to find out about it and will come to my office, I will tell him. My hon. friend knows the legislation is there. They have made use of it. It was put there for a purpose.

passed in Canada or Prussia?

Oh, not in Prussia. I
would not for a moment compare Prussia with Ontario. It would not be a fair comparison. The Ontario methods go far beyond the Prussian methods when it comes to special class legislation and special interests.

Would my hon. friend
oblige me with the name of that Act?

My hon. friend who has just taken his seat has delivered a tirade of destructive criticism against the Government. Well, my

experience in this House teaches me that destructive criticism does not get a man or a party very far. Constructive criticism, on the other hand, is wholesome either for an individual or for a party. I shall not follow the hon. gentleman in his peregrinations through the charges he has laid against the Government. The conditions which confront us to-day in Canada are a sufficient answer for my hon. friend; all he has to do is to look at the savings in the banks and the general conditions throughout the country, the trade we have, compared with other countries, as a result of the war, and so forth to be convinced that he is wrong. I should like to make a few observations on the motion before the House, not particularly with regard to the territory that has been so well covered by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) wherein he touched on the iron ore, the coal and oil situation, transportation, cost of shipment, manufacture, and the amount of ores consumed. There is no doubt that iron and iron products consumed in any country are a fairly good index to the development of civilization in that country. I would rather direct my remarks to what might be termed the hinterland of Canada and the resources which may be found within that vast domain. After all, these great resources are tributary to the great river St. Lawrence and the lake basins at its head, which provide the transportation for the southern portion of Canada. The coal underlying the plains of the West, if it is possible to get it, may be conveyed to the head of the lakes where the iron ores exist and the limestones are, and it is possible that within the next few years we may have great smelting works in the vicinity of the head of the lakes. I hope it will be possible, in the not too distant future, to bring coal from the eastern provinces by our waterways to the interior of our country. You have Provincial Governments stretching across the country in the southern portion of Canada, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia; but the fact is sometimes overlooked by Canadians that away to the north of these provincial boundaries we have a vast domain of country, rich in natural resources and favourable for development so far as climate is concerned, and well endowed with waterways. I refer to that vast section of our country which stretches from the western shore of Hudson bay to the Alaskan boundary, the 141st meridian west- We have there a territory which is some 1,600 miles in length from east to 
west, and which is approximately 1,000 miles deep from north to south, a vast domain adjoining the western portion of which is the territory of Alaska owned by the United States. Just in passing I should like to refer to that territory of the great republic in order to support the argument which I am about to make with regard to the possibilities of the territory under our own Dominion. The district of Alaska was purchased by the United States from Russia in 1867, the year our forefathers confederated Canada. The Americans paid for that territory $7,250,000, and secured from Russia an area covering some
600,000	square miles. Pessimists of that day accused Mr. Seward, Secretary of State for the United States, who made the purchase, of throwing away $7,000,000 of good American gold in the Arctic ocean. They called it the Seward Ice Box, and said it would not bring a dollar to the treasury of the United States. Well, many years have passed, years as many as this Dominion is old, and to-day the territory of Alaska is a very valuable adjunct to the United States. At the World's Fair in St. Louis, there were two pyramids, one representing the gold produced from one mine, the Treadwell mine on the coast of Alaska, and the other representing the amount in gold which the Americans paid for Alaska. One pyramid represented $7,250,000, and the other $21,000,000-from one mine alone. The amount of gold and other metals which the United States have taken from Alaska has paid for that territory, I suppose, fifty times over, to say" nothing of the seal fisheries, the salmon fisheries, and other natural resources. The trade of the United States with the district of Alaska, during the year 1920, amounted to $107,000,000. Now, it would be a splendid thing if we had a territory as well populated and as far developed as Alaska, from which we could draw great natural products that could be exchanged for ou: manufactured goods. That is quite possible in this great hinterland about which I want to address a few words to the' House this afternoon. In this vast domain, some 1,600 miles long, as I have said, and 1,000 miles deep, there is territory enough and there are resources sufficient to carve out not one province but three, each as large almost as the three prairie provinces, and perhaps as rich, because no one yet knows what the potentialities of this immense territory are. It is drained by two of the greatest rivers of this continent, and indeed of the world. The Yukon river, which

has its rise in Canada, flows through the territory of Alaska, and enters into the Behring Sea; and the Mackenzie River, having its rise in Canada, flows for its whole length through our own territory into the Arctic Ocean. Both of these rivers are similar to the St. Lawrence, and dissimilar to the Mississippi river. The Mississippi river and the country around it are of such a character that from time to time the river overflows its banks in very destructive floods. Nothing of the kind occurs in the St. Lawrence for the reason that at the head of the latter there are great lake basins, which the Mississippi lacks. There are lake basins at the source of the Yukon, and also of the Mackenzie which control the flow of these great streams^ producing an even flow throughout the summer months. And this is a great potential fact in the development of our north country.
Some people here think that the climate of the north country is not suitable for either man or beast. Some years ago the Senate instituted an inquiry into the climatic conditions of the North Land. I have here a report of that inquiry, and I propose to quote from the evidence of Dr. (now Sir) Edward Stupart, the head of our Meteorological Branch, as the climate, and particularly the sunshine of the North Land, and more especially that section of country that is in the valley of the Mackenzie river. He says:
For the three summer months-
That is the three growing months-
-a vast area which includes western and northern Alberta, Northern Saskatchewan and the basin of the Mackenzie, almost to the Arctic Circle, lies within the isothermal lines of 55 degrees and 60 degrees. Throughout this whole region the percentage of the possible amount of sunshine seems to approximate 55, and as the hours of possible sunshine at midsummer range from 17 hours the latitude of Edmonton to 19 hours 30 minutes at Fort Simpson, it may be surmised that growth of plants and cereals may be even more rapid in the northern than in the southern districts.
My own experience in the Yukon bears that out: The growth of vegetables in the Northland is surprising to people who have not been there. Throughout the valleys of the Yukon and Mackenzie Rivers it may safely be said, Mr. Speaker, that we have a salubrious climate, a climate where people live and where they have been living for a hundred and fifty years, a soil which would produce the vegetables and the cereals to support a very considerable population. The natural wealth of Canada is drawn from four sources-the
forest, the farm, the fishery and the mines. All these sources of our national and our natural wealth, Mr. Speaker, are to be found in this great domain of which I speak. Cereals grow well in the Yukon. The report also shows that cereals grow well in the valley of the Mackenzie. It may be interesting to the House to know that wheat will grow and mature and ripen in the valley of the Yukon, as it does in the far north section of the valley of the Mackenzie. On one occasion I brought to the House of Commons and' placed upon the table for members to see a sample of wheat that had matured in the Yukon. After they had inspected it I sent it to the seed analyst or expert at the Farm here in Ottawa. When the return came back to me this gentleman informed me that he had sown one hundred seeds taken at random from that sample of wheat. I was very much interested- and I am sure the House will be equally interested-to know that one hundred seeds germinated-they were one hundred per cent virile. I do not know that all the wheat that could be grown in that Northern country would be so virile, but I am sure that it would be true of a very large proportion of it. I would like to place upon Hansard a few more extracts from this interesting report of the Senate which bears the title "Canada's Fertile Northland," and particularly with regard to the Mackenzie basin. The report shows that this basin is capable of sustaining a very large and prosperous population, that it has great possibilities as an industrial country; and says:
According to one witness, who has had exceptional opportunities for familiarizing himself with the country and its resources, there is in the Peace River section of this country as much good agricultural land fit for settlement, anad yet unsettled, as there is settled in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Albert to-day.
That is a very striking statement. The report continues:
At Fort Providence, latitude 62.30, about 400 miles north of Edmonton, splendid crops of excellent wheat, barley, oats, peas, and other vegetables are raised, while as far north as Fort Good Hope, within fourteen miles of the Arctic circle, or latitude 66.16 and 970 miles further north than the city of Edmonton, cabbages, onions and other garden vegetables are raised.
So much as to cereals. Now I come to touch on the forest resources of the Northland. On this point the report says:
The various sections of the Mackenzie basin possess great forest wealth, the spruce areas in the North extending to the Arctic sea.

This constitutes a tremendous reserve which may yet be tapped and developed, particularly now that we know that pulp and pulp products are such important commodities in the industrial world. The report goes on to deal with animal life and mineral wealth and, Mr. Speaker, it must be remembered that it is not the country at the head of the Great Lakes that we are dealing with; it is not in northern Ontario, or in Nova Scotia, or in British Columbia. The area which is capable of producing so much national wealth is hundreds of miles north of these great sections of our country. What does the report say about the Mackenzie river basin in that regard? It says:
The mineral wealth of this region is undoubtedly considerable, including deposits of coal, oil, copper, silver, gold, native salt, sulphur, ochre, sand suitable for glass making, tar sands, etc.
Some people wonder why it is that in those northern latitudes we have a climate such as we have. I am frequently asked how much snow fall we have in the Yukon, and frequently my questioners are surprised when I tell them that we have not much more than two feet. They wonder why it is. It may be interesting to the House to know that the climate of the west coast is governed by the Japanese current, the same as the climate of the British Isles is governed by the Gulf Stream. This current comes along laden with moisture. There is no part of the Pacific coast from Alaska to Mexico in which the mountains are more than six hundred miles from the sea. The moment that moisture laden current strikes those high mountains precipitation occurs and the result is we have very heavy snow falls and rain falls on the seaward side of that mountain range, and conversely on the landward side you had a dry belt and small precipitation in winter, and a small rain fall in summer. The same condition prevails in the Mackenzie valley with one other factor added, the Chinook wind, which tempers the winter climate there. Wheat grows there as well as in the Yukon and perhaps even better.
The first great wealth of that country to be developed will be its mineral wealth, and it was so in the Yukon. While the Yukon is capable of supporting a very considerable population, its great wealth so far has been mineral wealth. I have no doubt that in the valley of the Mackenzie, that section which lies between Hudson bay and Mackenzie river, the oil and the asphalt taken from the tar sands will be the first products to any extent. I say that

the mineral wealth will probably be the first to be produced. Mr. Speaker, within the last twenty-five years-which is only a short time in the history of a nation- many important things have happened in connection with minerals in Canada. It is quite possible history will repeat itself in the next twenty-five years. It will be twenty-five years ago, on the 17th of August next, since gold was discovered in the Klondike. Since that time the Klondike has produced $200,000,000 of the yellow metal which has come out in a continuous stream and has enriched the countries to the south and particularly the western provinces of Canada. The finding of that gold opened up to us a storehouse locked, padlocked, by nature. But the finding of the gold caused an influx of people into the Yukon, and notwithstanding that the gold development has been lessened there is still a considerable population there. Within the past twenty-five years the Cobalt field was discovered in Ontario, a field which has given to Canada and the world about $200,000,000 of silver wealth. I suppose within the last fifteen years the Porcupine field has been discovered, and it still continues to pour out annually enormous quantities of wealth in the shape of gold. Our geologists tell us that the same rock which underlies the Cobalt and Porcupine regions extends to the far north, and it is quite possible that there may be other Cobalts and other Porcupines within the Arctic Circle. Even another Sudbury may be discovered there, because I am informed that as far west as Manitoba nickel deposits are found. There is no doubt that there are many other Klondikes in the Yukon, but whether they will be discovered in our time or not is in the lap of the gods. But inside twenty-five years, only two and a half decades, there must have been pretty nearly six hundred million dollars of wealth produced from these three camps.
If the oil discovery which was made last summer at Fort Norman is half as good as we are led to believe, it is quite possible that that immense wealth which I have mentioned may be trebled or quadrupled in oil.
I shall not detain the House to refer to the authorities I have in my desk, but Mr. Camsell, of the Geological Survey, states in his report on the tar sands of Alberta that there are at least 150,000 square miles overlaid with these tar sands, (ridh in asphalt, rich in oil, and rich in tar. The potentialities of mineral wealth of this great north country are almost beyond belief.

Alberta
coal, for instance.

Alberta has a great coal area. It is said that that province has more coal within its four corners than any other area in this sphere on which we move and live. I think that is true, but I am speaking of the country beyond the northern boundaries of Alberta and the other Western Provinces, and in asking the Government to consider the evidence that I am submitting to the House and to them, I hope they will not confine their investigation altogether to the southern portion of our country. We are often told that Canada is broken in the centre, it has a weak back. You have your coal resources on the Atlantic, you have your coal resources in the West, you have your settlements in Quebec and in Ontario, and on the plains, but in the centre where you should be strong you are weak. And if you look at the map, Mr. Speaker, that is only too obvious. But I say to you, Sir, that within the lifetime of men who are in this House there will be a new territory opened up away beyond the borders of the Western Provinces to-day which will produce great national wealth and will strengthen the backbone of Canada where it is now weak.
I suppose it is likely that the mineral wealth of this country is the first that will be tapped. The discovery of minerals has had a very potent infl.uence upon the movements of the human race. I will not go off our own continent to prove that, Sir. When gold was discovered in California in 1849, I think I am safe in saying, there were not
10.000	white people on that coast between the Arctic ocean and the Mexican line. That was only seventy years ago, and to-day California is one of the great states of the commonwealth with a population of
3.500.000	or 4,000,000. Washington and Oregon were forests and British Columbia was a desert so far as the occupation by whites was concerned-it was certainly given over to the Indians at any rate, and there was not a soul north of that province. In 1856 gold was discovered in the upper regions of the Fraser river, which led to an influx of people into the north, and the great province of British Columbia was carved out of the wilderness. We all know what a strong support it has been to Confederation since that time. Forty years later gold was discovered in the Klondike, and the influx of people established that territory and gave to that wilderness in the north a great people with a stable government.
Since 1849 until to-day instead of only
10,000	people between the crests of the Rocky mountains and the Pacific coast there are I presume about 10,000,000 people, in three states one province and one territory very largely because of the discoveries of these precious metals in the rivers and valleys of that territory. All of this is quite possible to be duplicated in the far north in these river valleys which, I have not the slightest doubt, contain vast mineral wealth, because those regions have been examined by our geologists in a very slight way and they come back with reports that indicate the great potential wealth awaiting development.
I do not desire to dilate upon this subject. I just want to touch the mountain peaks, as it were, and in closing my remarks I wish to be consistent with what I said in opening, that a purely destructive criticism is, I think, rather negative, but that a constructive criticism is a whole-' some thing either for an individual or for a government. Therefore I propose to make a few suggestions in the hope that the Government may take cognizance of them, examine them and if they think them worthy adopt them.
I have a great deal of experience, Mr. Speaker, in living in frontier countries and in framing legislation for them. In my time I have had a good deal to do with giving to the Yukon territory, which I have the honour to represent, a set of mining laws. A former minister of the crown, Hon. Mr. Oliver, for whom I have a profound respect, was a frontiersman and realized the necessity of having stable laws if the mining industry of the Yukon was to be developed, and during his regime I submitted to him certain suggestions, which were subsequently incorporated in the Yukon Placer Mining Act. Before that Act was passed there was no stability of title for the great basic industry there. Title was based on regulations passed by the Cabinet and capable of being changed by that Cabinet or by succeeding cabinets. Consequently we found it difficult to get capital to invest in our great mining industry, gold. The same condition exists to-day in connection with the oil regions in the Mackenzie river basin and all the other territory which is north of and in fact held by the provinces as part of the public domain. It is not good business for a government to grant oil leases based solely upon regulations. I hope as soon as the Government have the information necessary

they will frame an Act of Parliament which will give stability of title in oil leases. You will find, Sir, and our Government will find, that you cannot get capital to invest in an industry unless you have a good stable title, and that stability can be given only by Act of Parliament. So I hope the oil regulations which were recently suspended, but which I believe are now in force, will very shortly be incorporated in an Act of Parliament.

No
Act of parliament fixing regulations-not in their present form.

I am not sufficiently acquainted with the oil business to criticise the oil leases. If they were gold leases perhaps I could. But I notice my hon. friend from Edmonton has a resolution on the Order Paper, and I hope that when he discusses it he will suggest where the weak points are in the present oil leases. What I want is security and continuity of title, because oil mining is a little different from placer mining; it requires a very considerable expenditure of money, a good deal of time, and a high degree of skill to locate and develop these oil prospects.
We have here a Geological Survey which, I think, should be recruited up to full strength. I quite agree with what my hon. friend from Fort William said with regard to the depletion of the personnel of that scientific body during the last few years. I hope it will be recruited to full strength as soon as possible and that every man whom the Director of the Geological Survey can spare will go into that north country this summer and commence a survey of the territory which extends, as I say, from Hudson bay to the Mackenzie river. I know it is not possible to do this all in one summer, but I hope the work will be started at once, because it is of the first importance that prospectors going into that country should have geological maps so that they may know where to go to prospect for oil, and where not to go.
Here is another aspect of the question. We developed during the war some of the most famous airmen in the world, some of the most capable topographers and photographers in the world. We all know of the work, which they did in France and of the extent to which that work was valued by the military chiefs. These men are here, and if they are not in the Geological Survey we should get them, equip them with

topographical and photographic instruments, send them and their planes and their equipment to Edmonton or wherever the base is, and have them make aerial topographical maps of that vast country. It is of great importance that this should be done, because the eyes of the mineral operators are upon us to-day. Oil is king. We have struck oil in the north, and we want all the reliable information we can get for the people who are turning their attention to these nothern oil fields. It is necessary, therefore, that our geologists should go to that country this summer-and when I say this summer I do not mean that they should leave Edmonton in June when the river opens, go in there and stay from three to six weeks, and then have to start the return journey in time to come out before the river closes. That is what we have done in the past, because we could not do anything else; but we can do otherwise to-day. We are going to vote a considerable amount of money for our air services.

The river
opens in May, not in June. They are ploughing in Alberta to-day. Do not give our country a bad reputation.

I thank my hon. friend for the correction. Whatever may be the case in regard to the upper reaches of that river, I think there is a lake between the upper reaches and its mouth which does not open until June, and the oil fields are north of that. However that may be, what I am desirous of impressing upon the Government is this: I want these scientists whom we have, or whom, we can get, to go there and make a geological survey of that country, make a topographical survey and a photographic survey. And in doing so I hope they will not altogether neglect the Yukon.
Before I take my seat I should like to tell you about the new discovery of silver ore in the Yukon at a place called Kino Hill, 175 miles northeast of Dawson-a place which you will hear of during the next few years. Enormous deposits of silver ores have been discovered there as the result of the operations of geologists in that country a few years ago, whose reports indicat-ted the possibility of the discovery of silver ores. The facts have borne out the truth of that prediction.
We know nothing about the fisheries of ' this nothern country of ours; yet we have in the employ of the Fisheries Department one of the greatest living scientists, a man

85T
who knows more, perhaps, about fish than any other man in the whole world-Professor Prince. I would like my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) to sent Prof. Prince into that north country this summer to make a survey of the fisheries and to tell the people what the fisheries of that vast country are worth. We have had very assuring reports concerning them, but whether or not the conditions are as stated in the reports,
I do not know.
Let me point out also that when you place a community in one of these northern countries, a community whose members live upon the natural resources, you have a community which consumes the best goods that the Canadian people can produce, and who pay well for them; because in the early stages of every frontier settlement the people of these newly opened districts are great consumers. This is particularly the case in a mineral country and in an oil . country such as we expect to be developed up there. So I suggest that our Government do these things with the idea of opening up that vast country, because if they do they will considerably enlarge the map of Canada; they will bring about the establishment of communities which will be continuous in their life, which will produce their share of the commodities which we use, and consume their share of the things which we produce, and, generally, be a prop and a support to Canada in peace or in war.

Mr. Speaker, in my judgment this is one of the most important questions that could be discussed by Parliament at the present time, because it is linked up with some of the other problems which confront us-the problem of unemployment; the problem of our national debt. If it is possible for Parliament and for the Government to bring about a great development of our natural resources, the enormous latent wealth of the country, we would not need to be so much concerned about the future.
I might criticize the resolution as worded, for this reason: the natural resources of Canada are largely under the Jirection of the provincial authorities. In the Prairie Provinces, however, the Dominion Government still controls the resources, and I feel there cannot be a settled policy in connection with the development of our natural resources until it is finally decided whether the
5 p.m. control of these resources shall in the future be with the
Dominion or with the provinces. As matters stand at present, there is an uncertainty that holds back both the Dominion Government and the provincial governments from action that would help to bring about the necessary development.
Now, I am going to deal with two or three of what I consider to be the most important problems in connection with the development of our natural resources in the province of Alberta. A question was put to the previous speaker (Mr. A. Thompson) about the coal resources of Alberta. I asked the Director of the Geological Survey to supply me with the latest information as to the actual resources in coal of that province. He has furnished me with some figures that are startling, and I think the House would benefit by having them placed on Hansard. I quote from the statement:
