It may not be known to this House and to the country that Alberta contains about 86 per cent of all the coal resources of Canada, 61 per cent of the coal resources of the British Empire, and over 14 per cent of the coal resources of the world. I make that statement on the authority of the Director of the Geological Survey.
Some members of the House might like to have an idea of the actual production in Alberta. During 1920 Alberta produced over one-third of the coal produced . in this Dominion. It produced 6,859,346 tons, while Nova Scotia came second with a production of 6,395,545 tons. I have quoted these figures in order to give the House some information about one of the great natural resources of Alberta, but

probably during the session there will be an opportunity to enlighten the House further upon this question.
We have heard something about oil during this session, and from all that can be gathered, I think it is quite possible that one of the greatest oil fields in the world may have been discovered in the country to the north of the capital of Alberta. It may not, however, be known to this House and to the country that efforts to obtain oil are not confined to one section of Alberta, but that efforts are being directed in all parts of that province to discover oil. There is no wild-catting, no careless movement at all; men are putting up real money and making a real effort to discover oil in that province. In the neighbouring state of Montana a great oil field has already been discovered within a very few miles of the southern boundary of Alberta, and that discovery is lending encouragement, to prospectors and actual companies for exploration purposes operating in the southern part of the province, that oil will be discovered there.
We have every reason to be hopeful in connection with those two great resources in Alberta particularly. What I want, however, to direct the attention of the House to is a question that I have frequently brought to the attention of Parliament but which to-day, I consider, is much more important than it has been at any previous time. It relates to the development of our natural resources. It is known to this House, and largely to the country now, that great portions of the southern part of Alberta and the southwestern part of Saskatchewan have been settled, and the problem faces the people to-day whether they will be able to remain and make an existence upon the land, that is, in what is known as the semi-arid or arid belts of those two provinces,. In the light of history, I think it can be established that a mistake was made, in the first place, in opening up certain of the southern parts of those provinces. But they have been opened up; practically the whole of the country is settled; but through crop failures every few years, caused largely by drought, those people are not able to eke out an existence, and the governments of the Dominion and of the provinces have to come to their relief every few years. On account of the assistance that has to be granted occasionally by the Federal Government and on account of the fact that the settlement of that country was due to the activity and policy of the fed-IMr. Buchanan.]
eral power, this matter has become a question of federal importance. At this time, it is most important that the Federal Government should co-operate with the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta in appointing a commission to survey the agricultural resources of the southern parts of those two provinces and to decide what sections of them can be held for settlement and what sections should be opened up for other purposes. There is a solution of this problem, and it lies in the provision of irrigation, wherever that is possible, for the dry areas. We have had experience for many years with irrigation in Alberta, and wherever it has been utilized in those dry sections of the province, it has been a success. I hope to establish to the House this afternoon the real importance of irrigation in connection with the salvation of those areas in the southern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta that are to-day facing practical destruction as agricultural areas. We have at the present time in Alberta alone one million acres actually irrigated or in a position to be irrigated from works actualy constructed; 130,000 acres will be irrigated from works already designed and authorized, and 550,000 acres are believed to be susceptible to irrigation by works which have been planned and the construction of which may be authorized as soon as the necessary financial arrangements can be made. I do not want the House to gather the idea that it is possible, by means of irrigation, to reclaim all the dry land area in these sections of the two western provinces, because that is not the case. In the first place, there is only a certain quantity of water available for irrigation, and in the second place there is only a certain area of land that can be irrigated. It is estimated that, in the two provinces, it is possible to irrigate or reclaim and make sure of success for agriculture, 5,000,000 acres. I believe, with this area of 5,000,000 acres put under irrigation, a safeguard would be offered to dry farming on bordering lands. As the matter stands at present, when a drought strikes those sections of the West, there is no possibility of carrying along the stock during the fall, winter and spring months, because there is no feed; but with irrigation districts adjoining those areas, it would be possible to provide the feed and save the livestock, and that in itself is important in retaining the people on dry land areas in certain sections of southern Alberta, although I maintain there are other

sections where it is impossible to retain them even with irrigation or with irrigation adjoining.
The problems that face Alberta, particularly in relation to irrigation, I can outline in two or three paragraphs. First, there should be the most complete storage of high water and flood flow of all streams in southern Alberta and southwest Saskatchewan. Second, there should be an interpretation as soon as possible of the Waterways Treaty in order to ascertain the water that is available from international streams for use for irrigation purposes in the Province of Alberta. The other problem is that of finance. I might be asked-What business is it of the federal power for me to bring up this question of irrigation? Even if the federal power has no responsibility whatever in connection with the actual development of irrigation districts, the federal power is, at the present time, responsible for the surveying of those lands in order to ascertain whether they can be irrigated or not, and it is also responsible for the streams which would be used to water those lands. So, in that respect, the matter is one of federal importance, and it is of the utmost importance to that part of the country that the federal power should continue these surveys until it finds out how much of that country can be irrigated and how much water is available for irrigation purposes. The question of financing has reached a stage where the Dominion has placed the responsibility on the local authorities, and the question of finances is the most serious matter at the present time. Districts have been formed in southern Alberta, and they are in a position now that they can proceed to construct irrigation works if they can find the money to pay the contractors. I am not presenting a case for help from the Dominion, because the people who want these systems are prepared to pay for the construction of them with their own resources, but the trouble is that on account of lack of information about irrigation systems on the part of investment markets in Canada it is impossible to sell those irrigation bonds without some help from either the Dominion or the provincial authorities, and the Provincial Government of Alberta is being urged at the present time to guarantee the bonds in order that the money may be raised for this particular purpose. These districts are formed in a similar way to municipalities, and they can be bonded in the same way. I shall attempt to establish that it would be in the
interest of the country that these areas should be irrigated as quickly as possible in order that they might be made productive, and in order that the people there might be able to meet their obligations as citizens of this country.
In 1919 in the southern part of Alberta and the southern part of Saskatchewan, and in many other sections of Western Canada, practically no crop was raised on what we call the dry lands. Adjoining the city of Lethbridge there is the oldest irrigated section in Alberta, a territory that was irrigated by the old Galt Land and Irrigation Company, and afterwards taken over by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. In 1919 all the lands adjoining that irrigation district were burnt absolutely dry; there was no crop whatever. In the irrigation district the value of the crop raised on irrigated lands, good, bad and indifferent, was estimated by the Canadian Pacific Railway officials to be $54.71 per acre. I would like the House to keep that figure in mind, and remember at the same moment that on the adjoining dry lands there was nothing raised at all. If we could extend irrigation to the districts where it is possible to bring water and irrigate the land, these areas would produce agricultural wealth year in and year out. I might say that one section of country that had been formed into an irrigation district adjoining this Coaldala district of the Canadian Pacific, if it had had water in the dry year of 1919 it would on the same basis have produced $7,000,000 of wealth, but without irrigation it produced absolutely nothing.
This matter is of importance to this Government and to this House as it would remove the necessity for assistance to the settlers in these dry areas in the dry years by providing seed grain and relief to the settlers when they have no crop at all. It would also settle the question of mixed farming in that part of the country, because on irrigated land practically all classes of farming can be carried on successfully. There are members in this House from the province of British Columbia who know what it has been possible to do with irrigation in the arid sections of that province, and those of you who have followed the development of the arid regions of the United States know that there great areas of desert lands have been reclaimed by irrigation and are to-day producing great wealth. I have in my possession figures to show that in the case of certain of the irrigated projects of the Middle Western

I desire, in the first place, to congratulate the mover of the resolution on having brought it to the attention of the House, and also on the able manner in which he handled the subject. In considering what branch of this manifold subject I should speak on myself, I found a good deal of difficulty. The resources of Canada are so numerous, so wonderful, and so great in extent that it is hard to decide, on a motion of this kind, to which particular resource one should confine discussion. However, as I am particularly interested in fisheries I thought it would not be out of place for me to offer a few remarks on that subject.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that any policy brought forward by the Government for the development of the natural resources of Canada should cover the question of greater efficiency in the development of our fisheries, for they are worth the most earnest consideration. In 1919, the fishery products of Canada amounted to $61,363,502, and in 1920, $56,508,429. You will observe there was a decrease of some millions in 1920 as compared with 1919. The fishery exports of the Dominion in 1919 were $37,137,102,
and in 1920 $42,285,055, an increase of five millions. It seems to me that where we have a resource which gives rise to such a large percentage of exports we should do something to develop it. In British Columbia, the fisheries constitute a very important part of our natural resources.
In 1919, the value of the fisheries production was $25,301,607, or 44 per cent of the production of the entire Dominion. You will agree with me, then, Mr. Speaker, that, representing as I do a British Columbia constituency, I have a peculiar right to speak on this important subject. I do not agree with the hon. member for Pontiac, (Mr. Cahill), in the view that in speaking on this resolution I am in anyway criticizing the Government, nor do I think that it was the object of the resolution to provoke criticism. I think that as members, on private members' day, we have a perfect right to bring to the attention of the Government such matters as we think worthy of consideration. I do not agree with another thing which was mentioned by the hon. member for Pontiac. I took it from his remarks that he is in favour of an open door for immigration. I certainly agree, as I suppose all other hon. gentlemen will agree, that immigration should be encouraged, provided we get the right kind of immigrants. I think it is important at this time, when there is so much unrest throughout the world, when the eyes of the world are turned towards Canada, and when we may expect large numbers of people to come into our country, that we should see that the right kind of people come to Canada. That is very important, and I entirely agree with the policy which the Government has adopted in that respect of strictly examining all those who wish to enter this country. Now, it may be that my hon. friend desires that certain classes of people should come into Canada who would not be wanted here; and I have in mind that possibly he may desire that certain immigrants from a part of the Empire where there is a good deal of trouble at the present time and who are going in such large numbers to New York and other American ports, should be given free entry into Canada. If that is his idea I certainly do not agree with him.
Now taking up the question of the fisheries I wish to say that I do not desire in any way to criticize the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne). As a matter of fact I would congratulate him upon the manner in which he is carrying

out his duties, and upon the attention that he is giving to this important industry. I think I can tell him that those who are interested in the fisheries in the province of British Columbia appreciate very much indeed what he has done and is doing to encourage the fishing industry. Shortly before I left New Westminster I had the privilege of attending a meeting of white fishermen of the province, and at that meeting the president of the association stated that the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries had done more for the fishing interests than had any previous minister. I have no complaint to make either about the fishery officers. I believe that they have been efficient, that they have been doing good work, and that they are good and capable men, but I think that something may be said as to the system under which they have been operating. It is generally conceded, for instance, that on the Fraser river, which at one time was the greatest salmon fishery river in the world bar none, the salmon fisheries have depreciated to such an extent that the people of that country gravely fear that unless something is done the Fraser river will cease to be a salmon stream of any consequence. In fact as one of the fishermen at the meeting I have referred to put it: "If things go on as they have been going, in a short number of years there will be nothing but bullheads in the streams and boneheads on the banks." On a previous occasion I gave some details as to the decrease in the pack of salmon on the Fraser river and I do not intend now to repeat them. I shall, however, offer a few suggestions for the consideration of the minister.
My first suggestion has reference to the propagation methods which have been in use, in the province of British Columbia at all events. Results are what count. The important point is not the output of fry, but the number of mature fish that return. The hatcheries have been operating in British Columbia at the expense of many thousands of dollars a year for many years past. Millions of fry have been turned out at these places with the expectation that they should go out to sea and in due course return as fully grown fish, but unfortunately no results have been obtained. Therefore there must be something wrong with the system. What I submit-and I think I have a good deal of authority for my contention-is that the whole system of hatchery operation has been carried out on the wrong basis. The 
operation of hatcheries and the propagation of fish has not been according to natural methods-it has been entirely artificial. Now I submit that what is required is a combination of artificial and natural methods, and there should be a return as much as possible to nature. I have before me an article which appeared in the Canadian Fisherman, of September, 1919, which I think sets out the situation better than any words of mine could. I-therefore, with the indulgence of the House, propose to read this article:

maintopic: A NEW ANGLE TO THE SOCKEYE SALMON HATCHERY QUESTION.

speechtext:
Mr. Henry Doyle believes Hatchery Methods can be improved on.
The following statement and interview by Mr. Henry Doyle of the Northern B.C. Fisheries throws new light on sockeye salmon hatchery methods, and opens up an altogether new angle to this important question. Mr. Doyle's Ideas will be read with great interest, as he is a pioneer in the salmon canning business of British Columbia and has made a careful and exhaustive study of salmon and their habits.
Mr. Doyle believes that hatchery operations on the Fraser River have been mainly responsible for the depletion of the sockeye salmon.
That fry liberated in rivers and streams that are lake outlets, have been a total loss. Reforms in hatchery operations, modelled more closely on nature's own lines, would, he believes, aid the increase of the sources of supply in the fisheries of the province.
With due respect to the men who believe otherwise and have made statements on the subject recently, Mr. Doyle said he believed sockeye salmon hatcheries operating upon the right lines would prove successful.
"Just because there has been an apparent failure in sockeye salmon hatchery operations under present methods, does not necessarily mean that the entire system is worthless," he said. Mr. Doyle does not think that hatchery work should be discontinued until the improved methods have been tried out. He suggests that officials .in charge of hatchery operations sometimes lack efficiency. He said. "The failure of hatcheries to procure any augmentation in the number of sockeye salmon in areas where the hatcheries are situated, is probably very largely due to those in charge lacking appreciation of the necessity of employing distinctive methods for each individual species of fish. One who makes a success of whttefish hatching and applies similar methods to salmon propagation would make a mistake, and even in salmon culture the method of treatment for spring salmon must differ materially from that employed with the sockeye species."
Mr. Doyle's statement on sockeye salmon hatchery methods follows:
"Spring salmon deposit their spawn in streams which flow directly into the sea. A sudden transmission from fresh to salt water would be fatal to the young fish. Nature, therefore, endows them with size and strength to maintain themselves in the blackish water at tidal levels until sufficiently acclimatized to exist in the sea. Sockeye salmon on the other hand, spawn , only in rivers having a lake source, and generally then in the small streams by which the lake is fed. This distinctive feature in the natural laws governing the spawning habits of the two

species indicates that different methods should be employed in artificial propagation work, but in the past this very important factor has been almost completely ignored.
"Sockeye salmon propagation on the Fraser river commenced in 1884 and year after year eggs were secured from Silver and Morris creeks and other tributaries of Harrison lake. When the fry were being planted they were mostly deposited in the Harrison river, which Is the lake's outlet, where the current of this and subsequently of the Fraser river would carry them to the gulf of Georgia before they found suitable currentless water in which to remain while attaining greater growth. In the fry stage sockeyes lack sufficient strength to hold their own against the sweep of the tides, and doubtless practically all perished from too sudden change from fresh to salt water.
"Dr. Charles H. Gilbert, of Leland Stanford University, is unquestionably our greatest authority on salmon life, and his investigations have shown that practically no sockeye, reaching the ocean as fry, return to the rivers as mature fish. It therefore follows that sockeye fry liberated in rivers and streams that are lake outlets have been a total loss.
"Hatchery troughs", continued Mr.	Doyle
"have smooth sides and bottom and offer no opportunity for the young fish to hide, and Mr. A. Robertson, officer in charge of the Harrison lake hatchery, has pointed out that fish raised therein at least partially lose the natural instinct to bury themselves under gravel when danger threatens. Indeed, he says, they come to know the attendant that feeds them and swim toward him when he .appears with their food. It stands to reason that such fish, even when deposited In the waters of a lake, will fail to protect themselves against their natural enemies, and, lacking the instinct to seek shelter, would doubtless swim around until entering the current of the lake outlet, they would be swept seaward and likewise perish in their fry stage upon reaching salt water.
"Practically all the fish reared in the Harrison lake watershed have been liberated as fry in either the lake or the lake outlet. Few, if any, were planted in the streams flowing into the lake from which in the past the parent fish were secured. If my theory is correct, it follows that practically all those produced by hatchery operations have been lost, but in addition, and more important still, stripping the spawning streams year after year of the parent fish, with no attempt made to replace them with hatchery fry, has eliminated natural propagation as a factor in those streams.
"Years ago the Harrison lake watershed was the main spawning area of Fraser river sockeye; to-day its spawning beds are deserted while mature fish pass them by to ascend the Lillooet and Berkenhead; and I believe the depletion of these streams and the consequent diminution in the quantity of salmon in Harrison lake is largely, if not entirely, due to hatchery operations.
"But while the past has ueen disastrous, the future seems bright. The spring salmon hatcheries of the Columbia and Sacramento rivers have been successful in restoring the runs on those rivers, and all conversant with conditions in those waters know this to be the case. It only remains for us to ascertain the proper procedure for sockeye propagation when success with that species will likewise surely follow."
Mr. Doyle refers to the success which has been had in the Oregon fisheries. As a matter of fact, on the Columbia river they had almost the same experience that we had on the Fraser river, and in 1895 they were practically in the same position there as we are on the Fraser river to-day, that is, their run of salmon had decreased to suich an extent that everybody was alarmed and it was feared that the whole stream would be depleted. The Oregon authorities have been studying the subject for some years, and they have worked out a system which, it seems to me, could be very well applied to the Fraser river; and not only to the Fraser river, but also to all the other rivers and streams in British Columbia where the sockeye runs. Their scheme was the building of retaining ponds. According to our methods of hatching salmon, the fry was turned out after a very few months when it was very small and not able to protect itself from its natural enemies, or to withstand the action of the salt water. In Oregon they built a very large retaining pond- of course, a great many of these retaining ponds were built-and then the small fish were kept in those ponds until they were a year and a half old.

speechtext:
Fresh water. Then the fry were turned out to sea. They were turned out not into an outlet of a lake, as was the case with us almost universally, but into a stream-a gravel stream preferably-which led into a, lake. The fish were at an age when they knew something and were able not only to protect themselves, but their instinct was sufficiently developed to prompt them to go out to sea and to come back. The fisheries on the Columbia went from bad to worse until very lately-I think it was about a year or so ago-and a great deal of discontent followed as to the method which they were trying to work out there. But when sufficient time was allowed for these small fish to come back, they found that they did come back ift the shape of larger and better fish than they ever had there before, and in such increased numbers that the run approached the greatest run ever known on the Columbia river. At the present time that river has come back to its own, and other rivers and streams in Oregon have also come back to their own, so that the fisheries of that state have been restored almost to normal. What has been

done by the Americans surely can be done by us, and I submit to the minister that the system in use in Oregon should be studied very carefully by his staff, with a view to its application to the province of British Columbia.
Another point in connection with the hatcheries is that it seems to me where we are hatching out fish, as we do on the Fraser river, while the Americans in the state of Washington are doing nothing in the way of propagation and are getting our fish, they should be required to assist us to some extent in maintaining our hatcheries. I think that is only reasonable, and I believe if suggested to them in the right way they might be prepared to assist us.
Another suggestion which I should like respectfully to make to the minister is that the administration of the fisheries should be reorganized. At the present time everything is run from Ottawa. Now, although they have competent men here, they are a long way from the Pacific and they are a long way from the Atlantic. I submit that we should have both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific local |boards which should act in an advisory capacity, and, if possible, have executive powers. This is not a new suggestion; the matter has been put before the department more than once. It was discussed very thoroughly before the Royal Commission appointed by the Government in 1917 to investigate fisheries conditions on the Pacific Coast. In the report of that commission the matter was dealt with as follows:
Your Commissioners are of opinion that the plan of organization of the administrative system should be reconsidered with a view to making it more effective in dealing with the important problems of the Pacific fisheries. The outline sketch of the present system, given in the introduction, does not reveal practical coordination among the various related services under the control of the Dominion, and there is, moreover, the problem of the overlapping activities of the Dominion and the province. The system is characterized by extreme centralization at Ottawa, and yet only in the Minister of the Naval Service does it there find unity, there being no one official in Ottawa, exclusively assigned to fishery problems, in whom centre all the administrative activities directly affecting the fisheries. On the Pacific Coast there is no connection at all between the different services and the powers of local officials are strictly limited. In the inspection service, for example, although the local inspectors may issue renewal licenses to licensees in good standing, apparently almost everything else must be referred to Ottawa for decision.
The fishing interests have made many representations in favour of more immediate access to executive authority. What is now known as the Pacific Committee of the Advisory Board does not meet the particular need felt. This

Pacific Committee consists of the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service, chairman, the Commissioner of Fisheries, the General Superintendent of Fisheries, the Assistant Superintendent of Fisheries, the General Inspector of Pickled Fish, who are all officials of the Department at Ottawa, and the Chief Inspector for British Columbia and a representative of the provincial administration, the Deputy Commissioner of Fisheries; and there has recently been added one non-official member, a resident of the northern part of the province. In so far as this committee makes an occasion, once or twice a year, for certain higher officials to sit in conference, it is valuable, and the presence of the representative of the Provincial Department of Fisheries is of importance, but it is, in the main, only a method by which these officials work out their problems; it does not bring together all the higher officials of the services bearing on the fisheries: and it does not alter the general nature of the system nor create a local organ.
At six o'clock the House took recess. .
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: A NEW ANGLE TO THE SOCKEYE SALMON HATCHERY QUESTION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose, I was reading from a report of the Royal Commission on Fisheries, 1917, and I would like to read just this further short extract from that report:
The Pacific fisheries have been producing about 40 per cent dn value of the total fishery output of the Dominion, and are capable of great further development. The administrative system clearly should be so adjusted as to operate directly, comprehensively and effectively on the spot; for, as has already been emphasized, the fisheries are a great business and the constitutional position is such that the adiministrative system must determine, almost from day to day, the conditions under which the business can be operated. Mere changes in organization will not, in themselves, ensure constructive and efficient action and those responsible for results can best shape the instrument they will use. If a local organization is created it might centre in an individual who under the authority of the minister could coordinate and direct the local operations of all the different services related to the fisheries, or in a commission, which might include in its membership one or more capable business men with local knowledge.
Larger expenditures will be required even under the most efficient organization, but any wise expenditures will be comparatively small outlays to bring about the increasing national returns, wliich this highly productive industry can be made to yield. Increased provision should be made for scientific investigation, and it would seem most desirable that the scientific experts should be brought into more direct relationship to the practical daily problems. The present inspection staff is undermanned even for the work now undertaken.
In this report other matters are dealt with, but as I have now taken up a little more time than I expected, I shall not refer to them particularly. They all tend to

point out that the fisheries of the Pacific coast can be greatly developed, and, I presume, the same thing would apply to the Atlantic fisheries, and also, no doubt, to the inland fisheries.
The request for a local board on the Pacific coast is very general; it is advocated by the fishermen, boards of trade, business interests, cannery men and, I might say, practically the whole community. We feel we are so far away, that it is very difficult under present conditions to make the necessary progress. The feeling which exists at the present time amongst all those interested in fisheries is a very good one, and I think they are all working and striving towards the same end, which is to increase the fishery output of the Pacific and also to improve the methods of propagation.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) last session made some remarks derogatory to the cannery interests. He stated, I understand, that they constituted a big monopoly, and from his remarks one would infer generally that they were rather unfair in their operations- This is the first time that I have had an opportunity of saying anything on the subject, and I simply want to put myself on record as being opposed to the views which the hon. member for Skeena apparently holds. The cannery men have invested in that business a large sum of money running into something like fifteen million dollars or so; they are good businessmen, good citizens; they are carrying on legitimate businesses, and I do not think they should have been subjected to the criticisms which the hon. member made last session.
I have said that the request for this board is backed by practically the whole community. In April of last year, a delegation representing the Vancouver Board of Trade and the British Columbia fishery interests came to Ottawa and presented to the minister a memorial in favour of this board, which memorial I would crave the indulgence of the House to read, because it states the situation very well and gives the views of the people of British Columbia. This memorial, which is dated April 30, 1920, and addressed to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) reads:
For years those interested in the fisheries of British Columbia have urged your department to appoint a local board to control and administer the industry. It is felt that many of the problems which have given your officials great concern, and have been very disturbing factors to all engaged in this branch
55	!
of our natural resources, might easily have been adjusted if dealt with by a competent local board that was familiar with all the various phases which entered into the questions requiring adjustment.
The lack of such a local board compelled the submission of these matters to Ottawa, where only the leading aspects of the case would be known to your officials and their decisions, based on those leading issues, only partially dealt with the trouble. Adjustments which ignored the minor features of these problems often opened the door to a host of small complaints which grew in volume the longer they were neglected, until eventually they constituted grievances which affected the whole province.
In asking for this board, we do not wish to cast any reflection upon the officials of your department. We believe their decisions were only arrived at after giving the question deliberate and painstaking investigation, and that they honestiy believed their findings were in the best interests of the fishing industry of British Columbia. We submit, however, that their lack of familiarity with all phases of the issues was bound to have an adverse influence on their judgment, and that this is always to be expected when questions of this nature are settled by parties living three thousand miles away from the seat of operations.
Tou as a successful business man of large affairs know, from your own experience, how much better results are obtained from personal Interviews than from letter-writing. You can appreciate how points of major importance will be brought out in conversation which it would never occur to a correspondent to mention. Mail order houses unquestionably do a large business, but there is more satisfaction and less complaint when buyers and sellers come into personal contact.
In dealing with Ottawa we must necessarily rely on letter-writing for the presentation of most of the matters affecting the fisheries of British Columbia which require adjustment. Personal interviews involve the loss of too much time and the expenditure of money which often cannot be afforded. As an illustration of this we would mention the British Columbia Fisheries Protective Association and the soldiers' associations wished to send a delegate on this present occasion but were prevented by a lack of funds for the journey and because the loss of earnings for their delegate would also have to be compensated for.
As corrobation of our contention that your officials are not fully cognizant of all the points involved in our fishery question, we would point out that your predecessors have, on at least five different occasions, sent commissioners out to investigate, report, and make suggestions for the guidance of your department in devising regulations for the British Columbia fisheries. We submit that this in itself is a confession of weakness in the present system.
I might mention, of course, that these commissioners were not all appointed by the present Administration, or by the Conservative Administration which preceded it.
The States of California, Oregon, Washington, and the territory of Alaska, all have fisheries problems similar to those of British Columbia. In the cases of California and Oregon control is vested in fishery commissioners



possessing full administrative powers, and the industry in these two states is flourishing. Not only are there no contentious questions requiring settlement, but through intelligent, artificial propagation work the fisheries in their waters show actual increases. Shad have been introduced into the waters of both states and to-day California annually ships many carloads of shad to supply the demands of the eastern markets, while Oregon has worked up a successful business in canning this species.
As to salmon, California, after sixty years of strenuous commercial fishing produces more than it did in the beginning, and the Oregon Fish Commission advise us that "Columbia river and several of our coast streams have been holding their own, due to no other reasons, except that there has been a large number of good, healthy, advanced fingerlings turned into the same annually."
The State of Washington has the control of its fisheries placed in the hands of one fish commissioner. This man voluntarily asked that his office be made subservient to a fisheries commission "empowered to regulate fishery operations to the extent of saying how, when and where they may be carried on, and with ample authority to enforce such regulations." He adds: "This commission should take the place of a fish commissioner, for the power to be delegated by the legislature should be to three or four men rather than to a single individual. It can be elective or appointive, and should be apart from politics or partisanship; free to act solely for the interests of the state in rehabilitating and perpetuating a great natural resource-now approaching destruction."
I might say here that the State of Washington has now placed its fisheries under a local board.
The laws and regulations governing Alaska's fisheries are in the hands of the Federal Government. The law provides that before any change of regulations are made, public meetings must be held at Seattle, San Francisco, or in Alaska as best suits the convenience of those directly interested, and the subsequent requlations are based on the evidence submitted at such meetings. In addition, the newly prepared Alaska Fisheries Bill was determined and drafted by a local board appointed by the Federal Government for that specific purpose.
In New Zealand, in Scotland, in Norway, and we believe also in France and Portugal, the control and administration of the fisheries is vested in local boards. Not only have these boards become strong factors in fostering and building up the industry, but in all these countries the operations of the industry are carried on much smoother and more effectively than is the case in British Columbia under the methods in vogue there at present.
As previously mentioned, California and Oregon, operating under local boards devoting all their time and energies to the purpose, are showing increased production through artificial propagation accomplishments. Washington is asking for a local administrative board so as to secure the same effect. Washington's case is similar to ours, except that their propagation work is farther advanced and their methods more efficient. Artificial propagation in British Columbia has been a notorious failure; the methods employed are obsolete; and instead of making efforts to modernize the system, more money is now being spent to perpetuate the old policies.

British Columbia has a coast line of over 7,000 miles. Along this coast are over 1,000 streams, each possessing its individual runs of salmon. Excessive fishing in each and all of these streams means extermination of the runs unless the commercial depletion is offset by re-stocking each stream with fish secured through artificial propagation. It is not in the public interest to confine the industry of the future to Fraser and Skeena rivers. Rivers Inlet, and a few isolated points on Vancouver Island, where all your hatcheries are at present located. We must be just as particular to build up the thousand small rivers and streams, from which, in the aggregate, the most of our production is obtained. This means more extensive securing of salmon eggs ; the building and upkeep of retaining ponds for the resultant fry; some methods for properly distributing the young fish and some authoritative body that will oversee their subsequent development and welfare. It is out of the question for such work to be administered from headquarters three thousand miles distant; the present Vancouver staff have too many duties of their own to undertake work outside of their present sphere; the local administrative board has been found successful by our American competitors and we believe is the only feasible solution of the British Columbia fisheries problems.
It has been suggested you might be adverse to voluntarily handing over to such a local board as we ask for, the administration and control of the fisheries of British Columbia. We do not believe, however, you will view this question so narrowly. You have already demonstrated a broader-minded policy by diverting some of the Ottawa work and responsibilities to chief inspectors in Vancouver, Halifax and other points. This is the first step in the direction of the goal we are seeking. You have also divested yourself of the administration of operations of Vancouver harbour. It is only reasonable to suppose that if the direction of Vancouver harbour matters warrants the establishment of a local administrative board to operate and control them, an industry so vast and with such diverse and intricate problems as our fisheries contain, would be still more in need of local administration.
The board we are asking for is one that would be as fully administrative in every respect as is the Vancouver Harbour Commission. It would be non-political, and should consist of commissioners whose term of office would be sufficiently long as to give the industry the full benefit of the knowledge and experience they acquire. These commissioners should be three in number, one a bona fide experienced fisherman, one a practical cannery man, and a third, who would also be chairman, a returned soldier of qualified legal attainments. Neither the fisherman or canner commissioners should be permitted to remain interested in the commercial industry, and all should be provided with sufficient salary to make them independent.
In asking for the appointment of this board we are voicing the desires of the vast interests represented by the Vancouver Board of Trade; the interests of those engaged in the fishing industry in any and every capacity; and we are acting in the interests of the public at large. We do not wish you to look upon it as a plea from the salmon industry alone, for development upon proper lines, and under proper control, is just as much needed for our herring, pilchard, halibut and other deep sea fisheries, as well as our shell fishes. A local board dealing with this

newer development can avoid much of the mistakes which have led to friction in the salmon industry, and by carefully studying the situation from the heginning, can so regulate matters that the industries will be protected and production of new fish will keep pace with commercial demands.
The other fisheries referred to, cod, halibut, herring, whales, and all the other fish we have there, are of course very important. In British Columbia we have practically every kind of fish except lobster. We have no lobsters in British Columbia.
' Another suggestion I would make is that something should be done to eliminate the natural enemies of the salmon, and in this connection I wish to refer to the report of the Fisheries Commission before mentioned. I shall quote just a short extract:
The destruction of salmon, in various stages from the egg to the mature fish, by seals, ducks, eagles and trout is very great in the aggregate. Trout are very plentiful in the streams where the salmon spawn and consume large quantities of the eggs and the fry. The checking of this wastage is obviously in the interests of conservation. Witnesses before the commission did not, however, suggest very definite methods of dealing with the problem. Restrictions on the taking of trout for the market might be removed from salmon streams and the fishing of sportsmen encouraged; and at some expenditure by way of bounties, or otherwise, it is believed methods could be found for reducing the number of seals.
The most dangerous enemy of the salmon is the seal, particularly on the Fraser river. There are at the present time on the sandbars at the mouth of the Fraser thousands of these seals, and I am told that they are taking more fish than the fishermen themselves, and that they even' take the fish out of the fishermen's nets. This condition is not a new one, but I am sorry to say that nothing has been done of any practical value to meet the situation. Various half-baked schemes have been tried, but without any practical results. The seals are still there and, if anything, in greater numbers than ever. Something like two years ago the Department of Fisheries did try to do something in the way of destroying seals. They mined one of the sandbars, but it was very difficult to do much in that way, because as you all know, a seal is a very wise creature and it is difficult to put up any job on him. But after taking weeks, the officials finally succeeded in mining this sand bar. They were able to set off the mines when there *were a good number of seals there, and according to their report they killed about 500. I might mention that there was for a time a bounty on seals, but it was not large enough to encourage anyone to get after
55i
them for the reason that when you shoot seals the majority of them sink, and it is only once in a while that you can get one. In order to secure the bounty, you must produce a part of the seal-I think, one of the ears-in order to substantiate the claim that you have actually destroyed it. So that that arrangement was not very satisfactory. Now the fishermen have suggested that the proper method of meeting the situation would be the use of cross lines. These lines are, of course, dangerous to other species of fish, particularly to sturgeon. We have still some sturgeon in the river and in the lakes adjoining it, and some of these fish sometimes attain a weight of 1,500 pounds. This may possibly be regarded as a "fish" story, but it is true, nevertheless. The department has gone so far as to accept the suggestion of the fishermen, but in such a restricted way that it was considered by the men rather in the light of a joke. The department' offered to put on two crews of two men each, and allow them to use cross lines for one week. The fishermen do not consider that good enough; they are of the opinion that nothing can be accomplished thereby. They suggest, however, that during the months of December, January, and February they be allowed to use cross lines, and in addition, that they be given a bonus of $5 per seal. If that is not satisfactory to the department, then they urge that the department put on a number of crews and allow them to work there for three months. They claim that they would undoubtedly catch quite a number of seals and this would have the effect of intimidating other seals and inducing them to leave that district, because, as I explained before, the seal is very wily, and when he finds that the Government is really after him I have no doubt he will quit. I think that this is something that should be seriously considered. There is no question that the menace exists; and there is also the trout menace to cope with. This is serious, and nothing is being done in the matter at all. As a matter of fact, I think that trout eggs have even been placed in some of the lakes and streams in that district.
I would also suggest that something be done to build up a Canadian fishing community. This is something we have not got at present. On the Atlantic coast there are, of course, a great many fishermen who are good citizens and who help to build up the resources of the country, besides contributing to its population. In our country, unfortunately, the Japanese pre-

dominate; and although the Japanese fisherman is an industrious worker, he does nothing towards the building up of the country. Unquestionably he makes money out of the fishing industry, but most of it he sends away to Japan. Most of the Japanese keep themselves and their families on their boats. Of course, they can never be assimilated in this country.
According to the list which has been given me, a great many nationalities are represented in our fishing communities, but very few of them are Canadian; indeed, very few are British. This, I think is wrong. I think we should have a fishing community there composed of our own people, for Canadians should be given the advantage of our own natural resources. Of course, I understand that there is great difficulty in eliminating the Japanese, who apparently are there to stay; but it does strike me that it is not right that conditions should be such as prevail at the present time. If a number of Canadians went to Japan and predominated in any industry, as the Japanese predominate in the fishing industry in British Columbia, there would be some trouble over there, and it is safe to say that some means would be adopted to alter that condition. I am convinced that the fisheries of the Pacific Coast, of the Atlantic Coast, and of the interior, can be greatly developed under a proper system of control; and if you can double or treble the fishing products of the Pacific Coast, for instance, you will help your railways as well as your steamships, besides assisting a great number of our people. The bulk of our fish is exported. I have in my hand a card sent me from Prince Rupert, showing the number of fishing craft there at the docks, and on the back of it is written the following:
Halibut is marketed in Prince Rupert three times weekly. This photograph represents one day's arrivals. This shipment represents $17,000 to transportation companies and requires ex-aotly one-third of the available express refrigerator cars to handle.
If you take the whole shipment of halibut from Prince Rupert alone, you will find that many hundreds of cars are required during the course of a year from our national railways to take care of the transportation of this product. A large number of our ships could be used to take our canned salmon to other countries. I say, therefore, that to encourage the fisheries of Canada is to help in no small way to meet the situation with which the Government is now faced,-a large deficit in
[Mr. McQuarrte.J
the operation of its railways and steamships.

maintopic: A NEW ANGLE TO THE SOCKEYE SALMON HATCHERY QUESTION.
speechtext:
The importance of the subject covered by the resolution cannot, I think, be over-estimated. This fact has been demonstrated in the annual meetings of corporations such as banks and other financial concerns during the past few years. At almost every one of these meetings presidents and managers have given considerable attention to the question of the development of our natural resources. By way of illustration I would quote from a statement made by the President of the Canadian Pacific Railway at an annual meeting, I think, in 1919, as follows:-
With the vigorous development of the country's natural resources and the necessary extension of the markets of Canada, we have every reason for confidence in the future prosperity of the country.
This subject is one which, possibly, has been as widely discussed as any other before the people at the present time. It has furnished a prolific crop of speeches at general meetings of boards of trade, Canadian clubs, and public associations generally which have met during a number of years past in Canada. The question arises first as to the extent of our natural resources. We are accustomed to hearing the statement that our resources are unlimited. As a matter of fact, I doubt whether we know very much about what our natural resources really are; and it is doubtful also whether in some cases statements on the subject have not been very much exaggerated. At any rate, we know that our natural resources, whatever they may be, are of no use to us unless they are developed. They are no more useful to us than is a withered arm to a man. They do not provide work for the people; they do not provide wealth with which to discharge our national debt; nor do they in any other way assist us. Instead of having a policy for the development of these resources, we have at present a policy-if there really is one-which tends rather the other way. There are now handicaps that prevent the proper development of our natural resources. For instance, the present tariff, in my opinion, has the effect of retarding such development, rather than of assisting it. The importance of this development is set out in an article appearing in the Toronto Saturday Night:
Our resources are now our reserves. Not only are they owned by the citizens of Canada, but they must be employed to lighten the bur-

den of the war.* * * How all this is going to work out may only be imagined, but one would think that even If the state does not set up businesses for itself, it will have to reach down into business and see that our "great natural resources'' are developed into profitable enterprises, to the end that all the people will not go broke paying war taxes.
Now this is the sentiment which has been expressed far and wide. It is the sentiment which has been expressed already in this House and we shall hear more of it; but the point is that the expression of the sentiment has not got us anywhere up to the present time. What we now want is some active, definite policy which if pursued to the end will result in the development hoped for.
Before I enter further upon the consideration of this subject in a general way, I would like to bring to the atention of the Government a matter in regard to which I asked a question last year. The answer to that question was rather general, and in the light of information subsequently obtained, inaccurate. The question I asked had reference to the Economic Development Commission. I inquired when the commission was appointed, what work had been done and what its cost was. The answer given to me was:
No report has been made but the duties of the commission being largely suggestive and advisory, their views on certain subjects have been discussed informally with the Government for the purpose of advising or assisting the Government touching many subjects upon which it has been advisory to take action by legislation or otherwise.
The cost of the commission to that date was given as $23,200.48. The answer being so delightfully general, inconclusive and unsatisfactory I set myself to find out if I could not get information in regard to this commission from some other source, arid I obtained a copy oj( the Order in Council appointing it. The Order in Council is dated 28th June, 1915. I will not read it but merely mention in a general way what appeared to be the intention in the appointment of the commission. In the preamble it is stated:
The Prime Minister observes that the need is everywhere recognized of stimulating greater production in Canada.
A little further on there is this clause:
That before export the product should be converted through manufacture in Canada into the form in which it is proposed to be consumed or used.
Further on the question of the marketing of our food products is recommended to the commission; and later the question of
opportunities for a vigorous and effective policy of immigration is commended to the commission's consideration. Still further on it is set out that "transportation whether by land or water carriage, for reasons above indicated, is closely connected with the problems under consideration." It would appear from this Order in Council that the commission when it was appointed was given a sort of roving commission to investigate matters generally in connection with production and distribution.
To obtain further information I searched Hansard and found that the matter was brought up on May 9th, 1916. In reply to a question on that date the then Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden, said:
There have been reports made to me some times written and sometime oral.* * * I do however believe that a good deal of really important and interesting work has been done.
In conclusion Sir Robert Borden said:
I believe they will have a full report before next session.
The question again came up in 1917 in connection with an item in the estimates to provide for the expenses of this commission, and particularly in regard to the sum of $750 voted to Mr. E. H. Godfrey. In reply to a question by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) the Minister of Railways made this statement:
They have reports ready and these reports have been edited by Mr. Godfrey who was paid $750 for that work.
Now, Mr. Speaker, although I ' was informed last year that no reports had been furnished, yet at an earlier period two members of the Government stated that reports had been supplied and the gentleman referred to had been paid $750 to edit those reports. It would now be in order for the Government to explain these contradictory statements, give us the information asked for regarding this Economic Development Commission, and produce reports which are stated to have been made.
It may be that the commission in question was appointed to arrive at some policy along the lines of the resolution we are discussing. If that is the case nothing of the kind seems to have resulted from its activities. Surely the House is entitled to be furnished with some information as to how the $23,000 mentioned has been spent. It would appear to me that if we want an example of how not to do a thing we have a very fitting illustration in the case which I have cited.

The objects to be achieved by the development of our natural resources are briefly as follows: To create wealth; to provide raw materials for our industries and to adjust trade balances, I am not one of those who believe that the matter of exchange depends very much, if to any extent, upon the situation relatively regarding trade balances; but still it is always advisable to increase our exports as much as possible, and the development of our natural resources will help, to a large extent, to bring that result about. Another reason is that such development would have a tendency to put the West and the East in a similar position. I do not think that even in this event the West would depart from what it thinks is the proper policy to pursue in the interests of the whole country; but if manufactories spring up in the West and develop our natural resources, then the situation there would be similar to that in the East. And the West could not be accused of advocating a policy solely in its own interest.
The resolution calls for a definite policy in connection with our natural resources. I have not the temerity to formulate such a policy and hand it to the Government; but there are a few matters that I might briefly mention which I think should be taken into consideration in connection with any policy upon which the Government themselves may determine. In the first place I would advocate a systematic survey of the territory wherein lie these natural resources which await development. As I intimated previously we really do not know what we have in the way of natural wealth, and such a survey should necessarily precede the actual development. Already in this debate mention has been made of the work which the Geological Survey has done in this connection, and I desire to emphasize the remarks of the hon. member who made that reference-I think it was my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Thompson).
Unfortunately the Geological Survey Department at the present time is very much undermanned and underpaid. It has been doing a great work, particularly in connection with our mineral resources, in the way of pathfinding or pointing out where such resources may be found. But the staff of this department is very much below its normal strength, and in my opinion, not only should the staff be brought up to normal, but it should be greatly increased and the salaries increased also, because there is no question that more men

are required to carry on the survey, and by reason of the inadequate salaries many of the best qualified members of the staff have left the department to take more remunerative positions elsewhere.
Another illustration I might give is in connection with forestry. A little while ago in one of the forestry journals I read a statement to the effect that: There is no use at the present time trying to take up the subject of reforestation. The first thing we must do is to endeavour to protect the forests we have. We have immense stretches of timber and pulpwood, especially in the northern parts of Western Canada, and the amount of destruction by fire each year is really criminal. In my opinion the only way by which we can prevent this destruction is by the use of an aeroplane fire protection service. I will not go into details, but this work has been done very efficiently and very satisfactorily in the United States. I am corresponding at the present time with a young Canadian who had been in the Canadian Air Service overseas, but who when he came back to Canada found no opportunity of continuing his flying activities in Canada, and so took a position in the United States Air Service. He is now doing excellent work in California. He has told me what the Air Service is doing there in the way of fire protection-work that it is utterly impossible to accomplish except from the air. In northern Manitoba and Saskatchewan where there are hundreds of thousands of acres of pulpwood and timber only a few men are employed in the summertime in fireranging work, and it is utterly impossible for them to cover the ground thoroughly or to do anything in the way of controlling or extinguishing fires when they do break out. As many as a dozen fires are sometimes raging in a district extending over a distance of a few score miles in area, and the fireranging staff is utterly inadequate to cope with even one of those, fires. During the past twenty-five years one-half of the timber resources of that north country has been destroyed.
But a necessary prerequisite to any plan of developing these natural resources is the transfer of those resources in the western provinces to the provincial authorities. I do not propose to discuss this question at this time as there is a resolution on the Order Paper covering the point, btit until it is finally settled we cannot expect to have any definite policy agreed upon. The Federal Government has intimated that it pro-pqses to transfer those resources to the

western provinces, and, of course, if that is done there would appear to be no particular reason why a definite policy should be formulated by the federal authorities in respect to such resources and naturally the provincial authorities must wait until the natural resources are under their control before they can decide what policy they will pursue.
Another point that has already been touched upon is co-ordinating the development of our natural resources with the upbuilding of our National railway system. As an illustration I might mention that last year the Canadian National Railway built a branch line twenty-five miles northeast of Melfort, Saskatchewan, through a well settled country. Beyond this district is another area of good land which is not so well settled, being subject to flooding at certain periods of the year. This is known as the Moose Range area comprising about one hundred and nineteen thousand acres. When the railway is extended the best route will be through this area. The natural thing to do in connection with the extension of the railway and the development of the country would be to drain that area, and it could be done at a cost of about $2.50 an acre. When drained the land will be just as good as that through which the railway is already built and which is well settled. I understand, however, that although this project had been practically decided upon, the Estimates have been cut down so that it is not possible to undertake the work this year. Here is something which on the face of it the Government should take in hand in the interests of the whole country. This is a case where the expenditure of a few dollars will be returned a thousandfold, not only directly in the upbuilding and development of the country, but indirectly, which is just as important, in the furnishing of traffic for that railway; and with the extension of the line through this district it will be eventually well settled, and justify still further railway development. I will not pursue this illustration further, but it seems to me that at this particular time it is important to point out that we must co-ordinate the development of our country and the development of traffic for our railways. It is far more important that such development work as this should be taken in hand than that some other public works such as drydocks or canals be constructed.
I had intended to take up at some length the question of the development of our mineral areas, but I shall content myself
with merely referring to the anomaly that arises from the fact that although the Department of Mines is divided into two branches-the Geological Survey and the Mines branch-neither of them has anything to do with the actual mines or mineral areas, these being looked after by the Department of the Interior. Besides there is no mining law so far as the Dominion is concerned. Those who engage in mining have to depend on regulations which are subject to change from time to time. The situation is entirely unsatisfactory, and until the Federal Government enact proper mining legislation there can be no satisfactory mining development in the territory which is owned by the Dominion Government. The provinces of Ontario and British Columbia and the Maritime Provinces, and the states to the south of us, all have mining laws; but the federally owned areas which are known as mining lands are governed entirely by mining regulations which, as I have said, may be changed from time to time. Some one has said: it is better to have a poor mining law than good regulations, because then there is the element of permanency and the miner can govern himself accordingly. I might continue indefinitely on this subject, but I shall content myself by emphasizing the fact that one of the first things this Government must do if they wish mining to be developed in the territory over which they have control is to enact mining legislation along the lines pursued in Ontario or in British Columbia.
Last year I mentioned another matter which is of great importance not only in the interest of mineral development but to the returned soldiers, namely, the question of prospecting by means of parties of returned soldiers. It was stated by the Minister of Mines a year or so ago that such a scheme would not be feasible, but since that time it has been worked out in other countries. I understand that in Australia a scheme of that kind is now in operation; British Columbia also has a similar plan. I am not sure whether it is in force as yet, but in any case it looks feasible and I have no doubt that if it is not already in operation it will be put into effect very shortly. There would seem to be no reason why an interesting and profitable occupation should not be afforded our returned soldiers in that way, with the result not only of discovering but also of developing our mining areas.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) has mentioned the scheme in connection with reindeer outlined by Mr. COMMONS
Stefansson. Great credit should be given to Mr. Stefansson for the information which he has given to us in connection with the north country. We now know that the map of Canada has been rolled back many miles; that the north country, which has hitherto been looked upon as a vast, barren waste, is capable of supporting a considerable population and of producing as much meat in the way of reindeer and caribou as the southern country is producing by its cattle and sheep. I understand that Mr. Stefansson has already secured from the Government a lease or concession of some kind in respect to the southern half of Baffin island and that he is now purchasing reindeer to put on this territory in order to demonstrate the feasibility of the project.
I might continue indefinitely on this subject, Mr. Speaker, but I intimated that I would not take up very much time, and as there are other speakers on the programme and it is the desire, presumably, to conclude the debate this evening, I shall give way to the others.
